# CG Q11 # 

### TYPE YOUR CODE BELOW ###
# glimpse(brf)

I chose MENHLTH because it was a broader question and can connect easier with other subjects, cons percentage of data I can use is only 36% instead of 44%. 
### Then I looked at what possible variables can I use to predict it. I considered VETERAN3, because I am a Veteran, but it is not broad enough only 10% said "Yes". I looked at many others. Eventually, I decided what can possibly affect a person's mental health: money (INCOME3), age (_AGE_G), and physical exercise (EXERANY2).

# I used summary to inspect the distribution range and compared them to the codebook.
## summary(brf$MENTHLTH)
## The Max said 99 & NA's 2. Then, looked at the codebook. Noted that I need to clean: 99 "Refused", 77 "Don't know", 88 "None"   
##summary(brf$INCOME3)
## The Mean 23.22 & NA's 8847.  In codebook, looks like Categories 1-11. Noted that I need to clean: 77 Don't know, 99 Refused, BLANK.
## summary(brf$`_AGE_G`)
## no NA's listed. In codebook, looks like categories 1-6. Noted: need to convert to ordered factor.
## sum(is.na(brf$`_AGE_G`))
## Verified that there is no NA.
## summary(brf$EXERANY2)
## NA's 2. In codebook, looks like 1 = Yes, 2 = No, noting need to convert into factor.  Note: 9 = refused/missing need to clean.

Q11a <- brf %>%
  select(MENTHLTH, INCOME3, `_AGE_G`, EXERANY2) %>%
  arrange(MENTHLTH)
Q11a
## Line 203 I selected MENTHLTH as the response variable and my predictors are INCOME3, _AGE_G, EXERANY2.  
## Line 204 I sorted MENTHLTH because I just wanted it organized that way.

Q11b <- Q11a %>%
  select(menthlth = MENTHLTH,
         income = INCOME3,
         age = `_AGE_G`,
         exercise = EXERANY2)
Q11b
## Q11b I wanted consistent and lowercase names for easier reference throughout my coding process. I could also have used select to rename it 

Q11c <- Q11b %>%
  filter(!menthlth %in% c(77, 99)) %>%
  filter(!income %in% c(77, 99)) %>%
  filter(!exercise %in% c(7,9)) %>%
  drop_na(menthlth, income, age, exercise)
#view(Q11c)
## Removed 77 (response I don't know) and 99 (refused) from menthlth; removed income 7 (response I don't know) and 9 (refused) from exercise because they will not represent valid responses, because I am looking for number of days
## Used drop_na(), removed missing values because they did not respond, rather than if I put zero then it would throw off my stats because of inaccuracy, also I considered using replacing it with a min but I think that would throw off my stats too so I just decided to drop it. If I did end up using it I would've probably put the min on it and also the 77s, 99s, 7s, and 9s.

#sum(is.na(Q11c))
# checking if there are NAs
#Q11c
## verified that there are no NA's in Q11c

Q11 <- Q11c %>%
  mutate(
    menthlth = if_else(menthlth == 88, 0, menthlth),
    income = factor(income, levels = 1:11, ordered = TRUE),
    age = factor(age, levels = 1:6, ordered = TRUE),
    exercise = factor(exercise, levels = c(1, 2),
                      labels = c("Yes", "No")))
Q11
# I mutated menthlth by replacing 88 to 0, because it makes more sense to say zero mental health days for statistic calculations.  1-30 response provide number of poor mental health days, so my range will be 0 - 30 days.
# Mutated income into factor() order because they are category ranked. Income values are not dollar amounts, they are sorted by categories.  From codebook, value 1 is less thank $10K... value 6 = $35K to $ 50K... value 11 = $200K or more. Same reasoning with age: e.g, value 1 = 18 - 24 years old... value 3 = 35 - 44 years old... value 6 = 65+
# Mutated exercise to factor() with levels of Yes and No.
# Converted income, age, exercise to factor

nrow(brf)
nrow(Q11)
# There are 438,693 rows in brf, and after cleaning I retained 339,216 in Q11.

### Q11 Discussion:

1. Choosing four variables
###Q11 Discussion:

1. I selected four variables.  I wanted to look at poor mental-health days (respondent), and used predictors that can affect it (income, age, exercise). Once I figured my interest in mental-health choosing the predictors became easy. Finance, age, and physical activity are different variables that provides broad data and possibly whole picture of mental-health status.  

2. Meaning of each variable
- Mental health (menthlth) question was how many days during the past 30 days the respondent had poor mental-health. After cleaning, valid range of responses was 0 to 30 days.  I selected this first because it was broad and can connect to many things.
- Income grouped annual income into 11 ordered categories. Category 1 being lowest to Category 11 highest income. The data did not provide individual dollar amount for household income, so the data remained in categories.
- Age grouped age ranges into 6 categories, from category 1 age (18-24) through category 6 (65 and older). This limited my ability to determine the exact age of my respondent and only able to group them by age category.
- Exercise had two categories (Yes or NO), question was if the respondent participated in physical activity or exercise in the past 30 days.  I thought exercise connects to mental-health and wanted to investigate how it can. This does not show the intensity level of their exercise though as that can impact mental health too.

3. Levels of variables
- Mental health, measurement level is quantitative, discrete (ratio), numerical, with range counting 0 poor mental-health days to 30 poor mental health days.
- Income, measurement level is ordinal categorical, with 11 income categories, ordered factor, range counting lowest to highest.
- Age, measurement level is ordinal categorical, with 6 ordered age group, ordered factor, range counting 18 years to over 65 years old.
- Exercise, measurement level is nominal categorical, factor with Yes or No categories, not numerical of zero or one (I chose not to make it into binary but thought about it).

4. Response variable selection and justification
- Mental health (mnthlth variable). I selected this because I was curious about it and thought it would be fun to do research about it. Plus, mental-health is broad it can connect to factors (making it easy to pick many different predictors), and looked at the codebook responses for mnthlth and I prefered the numerical measures on the response and thought I can statistically work with, and broader than POORHLTH variable.
-  Income, Age, Exercise were selected as predictors because I wanted to see how it connects to mental health.  I knew financial stability and physical fitness affects mental-health but no data just common knowledge; for age I was curious how it can associate with poor mental-health.

5. Data cleaning and transformation
I used dplyr to clean and transform my data.  I renamed my variables to use easier names and lowercase to make it easier to reference throughout my project.  
Cleaning mental-health days - I removed responses with 77 (Don't know/Not sure) and 99 (Refused), converted 88 to zero because 88 represent no poor mental health days, leaving it numerical would be an error of outlier since range goes to 30 days.
Cleaning income - I removed responses with 77 (Don't know/Not sure) and 99 (Refused), converted it into ordered factor ranging from 1 to 11 categories.
Cleaning age - I converted age into a six category ordered factor, I was limited to categories because data did not provide exact individual ages.
Cleaning exercise - I removed responses with 7 (Don't know/Not sure) and 9 (Refused), and converted it into factor so it can be recognized as a categorical variable.

6. Data loss and its potential impact
After cleaning, I piped and used drop-na() to remove missing values in my mental-health, income, age, and exercise variables.  Ensuring my variables had valid information, I considered keeping them and replacing them with a min quotient but it did not make sense to do that as I think it will distort my data.  Dropping those missing values still gave me a substantial amount of observations. Final cleaned observation had a count of 339,216 (out of original data observation count of 438,693).
Also, I cleaned out the refused, don't know/not sure responses to only include valid responses. 
I acknowledge that removing or dropping observations could have created limitations like dropping na's gets rid of that respondent and could affect my analysis because I would have deleted other parts of their observation. I could delete it later, but I want the report to tie together from the start.  However, 339,216 observations remained which is a large sample size and sufficient enough to do my analysis to answer my question.

7. Overall discussion of cleaning decisions
Throughout the Q11 process I made notes in every single steps.  I was able to prepare my four variables by renaming, removing invalid responses, converting special codes, assign appropriate factor types, and drop missing observations.  Also, I kept mental-health response 88 and converted it into zero days of poor mental health, and to prevent it from showing as an outlier.
Furthermore, income and age remained ordered categories, and exercise was treated as a nominal factor.  I decided that to ensure proper calculations in my statistics and regression models.

# ***Exploring exercise & income, part 6 of 6 Visualization***
## In this visualization I wanted to compare mental-health days across the 11 income categories, income is an ordered categorical predictor with 11 levels and menthlth is quantitative response variable ranging from 0 to 30 days.  
## I chose boxplot to compare the median, quartiles, spread, and potential outliers across income groups. This will let me see the distribution of poor mental-health days across income categories.

# ***Visualization***
Q12_menthlth_income <- Q11 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = menthlth)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Poor Mental Health Days by Income Category",
    x = "Income Category",
    y = "Poor Mental Health Days"
  )
Q12_menthlth_income
## I noticed from the visualization that the average poor mental-health days decreased as income increased.

## I wanted to get the actual numbers. So I separated it by income categories, and calculated the number of respondents within income, mean mental-health days for each income, median of mental health, Q1, Q3, min, and max.  
Q11 %>%
  group_by(income) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(menthlth),
    median = median(menthlth),
    Q1 = quantile(menthlth, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(menthlth, 0.75),
    min = min(menthlth),
    max = max(menthlth)
  )
## I noticed a pattern where it is higher then down as the income got higher, this suggested that higher number of poor mental-health days are more common in the lower income groups. ### Q12 Discussion:

- I learned it was best to separate my processes by writing it into parts.  I started with looking at my data to see what I need to do.  Then wrote my processes into six parts, because I needed six graphs.  To create my graphs I used ggplot2.

Part 1 - Mental health (univariate)
To examine the distribution I used geom_histogram(), because the responses had 0 to 30 days, and selected a bin width of 1 to a whole day between responses.  Response for zero poor mental-health days was LARGE with 61.57% of the data.  Explaining why my median was 0 and mean was 4.21 days.  Interestingly, responses at 5, 10, 15, 20, and 30 days had small spikes, I suspected it was easy to report it by rounding their number of poor mental-health days.
Higher values like 30 poor mental-health days had 19,733 respondents.  It seems unusual to report that many days and examined if it was an outlier, I decided to keep it because it is a valid response in the codebook and could be valuable information later in my analysis.

Part 2 - Income (univariate)
To examine the distribution I used geom_bar(), because income was recorded in 11 ordered categories rather than exact dollar amounts. Category 7 had the largest number of respondents, with 58,660 (17.29%), while category 1 had the fewest, with 10,509 (3.10%). Categories 6, 8, 9 contained relatively large responses.  The distribution of the bar graph showed lower income categories contained lower distribution, middle to higher income contained larger distributions. The difference in income distribution when comparing to mental-health outcomes is important because higher income categories have more respondents than lower income categories.

Part 3 - Age (univariate)
To examine the distribution I used bar chart and scale_x_discrete for easier viewing of age ranges instead of their category codes of 1 to 6.  The respondents increased across the age categories.  Largest group responses was ages 65 and older with 113,064 (33.33%), next largest group was ages 55-64 with 66,445 (19.59%), smallest was ages 18-24 (5.14%).  
Responses showed older adults had a larger portion of my distribution, and younger showed smaller portion of my data, causing an uneven distribution.  Something I will need to consider when examining its relationship with poor mental-health days.

Part 4 - Exercise(univariate)
To examine the distribution I used geom_bar(), two categories regarding whether they exercised, choice of YES and NO.  76.45% reported Yes they exercised, and 23.55% reported No exercising. This indicated another unequal distribution and the variable is limited because it does not provide information on type or intensity of their exercise.

Part 5 - Mental health and exercise (bivariate)
To examine the distribution I used geom_boxplot(). I wanted to compare my poor mental-health days between those who exercised and did not exercise.  I chose a box-plot because I am comparing a quantitative variable (menthlth) across 2 level categorical answers (YES & NO). The box-plot allows me to compare find out why the responses of those that participated in exercise reported different numbers of poor mental health days compared with those who did not exercise.  
I noticed that average responses of those reported exercising had an average of 3.73 poor mental-health days, compared to 5.76 days for those that did not exercise, a difference of ~ 2 days.  Both groups had a median of 0, but 3rd quartiles were different.  The exercise group had a Q3 of 3 days, while the non-exercise had a Q3 of 7 days, showing a wider distribution of poor mental health days between the two.
The results suggested an association between exercise participation and fewer reported poor mental-health days.  However, this does not mean that exercise directly cause better mental health, because other factors such as age and income may influence it.

Part 6 - Mental health and income (bivariate)
To examine the distribution of poor mental-health days across 11 household incomes, I used geom_boxplot(), allowing me to look at the median, quartiles, variability, and potential outliers between income groups.
I noticed a pattern where it is higher then down as the income got higher, this suggested that higher number of poor mental-health days are more common in the lower income groups.  Income category 1, represents the lowest income range, reported average of 8.74 poor mental-health days, compared with 2.52 days in category 11, highest income range.The mean decreased consistently across all 11 income categories.
The Q3 showed a similar pattern, cat 1 and 2 had a Q3 of 15 days while cat 10 and 11 had Q3 of only 2 days.  This suggest that higher number of poor mental-health days were common among respondents in lower income categories.

Several potential outliers appeared in boxplot. I kept the observations because they are valid ranges like the 30 days in poor mental health category.  

Overall, this suggest a negative association between household income cat and the number of reported poor mental-health days.  Respondents in higher income reported fewer poor mental-health days than those in lower income categories.  However, this does not mean that higher income causes better mental health, because of other factors such as age and exercise.
Overall, my exploratory analysis showed that poor mental-health days were strongly right-skewed, with most reporting zero days.  My bivariate comparisons suggested respondents who reported exercising and those in higher income categories generally reported fewer poor mental-health days.  Also, my cleaned dataset had uneven distributions across income, age, and exercise groups.  I retained valid higher mental-health values despite their appearance as statistical outliers because they represent meaningful responses.  My observations provides a foundation for examining the relationships between my variables in later statistical models.

### Q13 Discussion:

1. Measures of center for each variable (menthlth, income, age, exercise)
- For menthlth, range of 0 to 30 days. the mean = 4.21 poor mental-health days, median = 0 (affected by the large number of 0 poor mental-health days observed), and total observations = 339,216. This result supports the observation in Q12.
- For income, ordinal categorical range of 1 - 11 (represent category of income ranges not dollar amounts, which then limited my ability to solve for the mean).  Median category 7, Modal category 7, Category 7 frequency was 17.29% of the observation. The income distribution is an ordinal income data, and observation is concentrated around the middle and not evenly distributed across the 11 categories.
- For age, it is ordinal categorical variable with six age groups. Median = 5 (55 - 64 years), Modal = 6 (65 years and older).  The median and mode showed older adults are the frequent representation. I did not calculate for mean because I was limited by the categorical data and was unable to convert it to individual ages. 
- For exercise, it is nominal with YES or NO responses. I only used the Mode = Yes, and it was not appropriate to calculate mean or median.  The two groups are unequal... Yes consisted of 76.45%, and No had 23.55%.   


2. Appropriate measures of variability. The different variables used different measures of variability.

- For menthlth variability, I calculated the following:
Standard deviation = 8.20 days (mean = 4.21 days, the SD difference is ~ 4 days.) 
Variance = 67.2 squared days, Min = 0 days, and Max = 30 days
Q1 = 0 days, and Q3 = 4 days, IQR = 4 days (indicating 50% of observations is between 0 and 4 days, this is due to the large number of 0 days reported and distribution is right-skewed)

- For income variability, I did not solve for standard deviation and var, because the income categories are ranges of income instead of actual dollars.  I did use the first (Category 5) and third (Category 9) quartiles to describe the 50% of data distribution between those two categories. Also used data from the most frequent category = 7 (17.29%), and least frequent category = 1 (3.10%).

- For age variability, I did not solve for standard deviation and var, because the age categories are unequal ranges of age instead of using exact actual years as observation.  I did use the quartiles: first (Category 3, 35-44 years old), and third (Category 6, 65+ years) to describe the 50% of data distribution between those two categories.  Also used data from smallest group = Category 1, 17,442 respondents (5.14%), and from largest group = Category 6, 113,064 respondents (33.33%).  This showed that my data set consisted more of older respondents.  

- For exercise variability, I only had two categories so I used frequencies and percentages. I did not calculate sd or IQR because it is a nominal categorical variable.  The result was uneven with group difference of ~ 53%, observation consisted of exercise group (Yes) ~ 76.45% compared to did not exercise group (NO) ~ 23.55%.

3. Bivariate statistics.
I used group_by() and summarise() to calculate bivariate statistics data with mental health across exercise and income. 
- For exercise and mental health bivariate, I compared the mean, median, standard deviation, Q1, Q3, IQR of the respondents that exercised and did not exercise.  The results showed that respondents that did not exercise ~ 2 more poor mental-health days average than the ones that did exercise.  Both had a median of zero and maybe due to the fact that majority of responses in the data reported zero poor mental health days.  There is a variability in the groups which showed the ones that did not exercise had a higher average of poor mental health days: For those that exercised, the standard deviation is 7.54 days and IQR of 3 days; in comparison to those that did not exercise, the standard deviation is 9.87 days and IQR of 7 days.
- For income and mental health bivariate, I had 11 income categories and the result showed a steady pattern of higher income, lowered poor mental-health. Income category 1 = average 8.74 poor mental-health days, versus Income category 11 = average 2.52 days, big difference and the variability steadily decreased across all the categories.  
In examining my bivariates, it supported my Q12 observations and good reason to use on upcoming analysis. 

4. Observations and Outlier analysis

I looked for potential outliers because of the large zero responses and a strongly right-skewed distribution.  To identify the potential outliers I used summarise for the quartiles, IQR, the 1.5 x IQR rule to see the lower and upper boundaries.  Q1 is 0, Q3 is 4, IQR 4, lower is -6, upper  is 10.  Since IQR measures the spread of the middle 50%, I calculated the upper boundary as 4 + (1.5 * Q3) = 10.  Since the valid range for poor mental-health days is 0-30, any response greater than 10 days was flagged as a potential statistical outlier.
I used summarise to calculate the total respondents, count the ones exceeded 10 boundary, and mean to percentage rounded to two. 13.43% (45,543 out of 339,216 respondents) showed as outliers. I decided not to remove the potential outliers because they are valid responses according to the codebook, removing them would eliminate 13.43% of data and exclude responses of poor mental-health days. I think keeping these potential outliers is important because they represent meaningful reports of mental-health experiences rather than indicating errors.  Removing them would distort my findings when examining mental health, income, age, and exercise.  I will keep all valid responses from 0 to 30 days for may Q14 answers.  I acknowledge that the large number of zero responses, right-skewed distribution, and high values may affect model assumptions. I will consider those characteristics when choosing my  next models.

# CG Q14 #

# *** Q14 Part 1. Model 1 - Predicting poor mental-health days using income ***
Q14_model1 <- lm(menthlth ~ income, data = Q11)
## In this portion I used lm() to create my first linear regression model to predict poor mental-health days using the income categories.  I used mental health as a response and income as my predictor, pulled the data from Q11.
summary(Q14_model1)
## I used summary() to display the regression results.
### Since income was coded as an ordered factor, R produced polynomial contrast coefficients to examine trends across income categories.  The linear component was negative and statistically significant (p < 0.001) supporting my earlier observations from Q12 and Q13 that respondents in higher income categories tended to report fewer poor mental-health days.
### The overall model was statistically significant (p < 0.001), but R-squared was only 0.031.  Meaning approximately 3.1% of variation in poor mental-health days are explained in income. Statistically, the low R-squared suggest that income has limited ability to explain differences in reported mental-health days.
### The residual standard error was 8.07 days, showing unexplained variation in the model.  My next approach is to compare this model to additional models (exercise and age) to determeine whether adding predictors improved the performance of the model.

## To better understand, I am revising model 1 to look at intercept, slope, p-value, and R-squared together.  This will help me examine whether linear model is appropriate by converting income categories into numeric values using as.numeric().
Q14_model1 <- Q11 %>%
  mutate(income_num = as.numeric(income)) %>%
  lm(menthlth ~ income_num, data = .)
### This revised model 1, I added mutate() to convert income from an ordered factor into a numeric variable so I could look at the overall linear relationship between all income categories and poor mental-health days.
summary(Q14_model1)
###  The result showed the intercept is 8.0457, and income coefficient is -0.571449.  It suggest that for every category increase in income, the predicted poor mental-health days decreases by ~ 0.57 days.  However, income categories are not dollar amounts and is a limitation treating income as numeric. I would love to be able to convert the income categories into estimated dollar amounts but my limitation is the data records would not provide the exact household income.
### The coefficient was significant (p < 0.001), suggesting a negative association between income and mental-health days.  This supports my Q12 & Q13 observations.
### Multiple R-squared of 0.02841, converting to 2.84% of variation in poor mental-health days. This was slightly lower than the original categorical model's 3.1%
### The results showed that income has a significant negative association with poor mental-health days, but the model explained only 2.84% of the variation when income is treated as numeric. I believe adding another predictor would improve my model performance.

# ***Model 1 Diagnostics***
# Model 1 - Residuals vs. Fitted
plot(Q14_model1, which = 1)
## I created this diagnostic graph of my regression model to identify the residuals against fitted values for Model 1.  Residuals represent the differences between the actual reported poor mental-health days and the values predicted by the regression model.
## The graph had vertical clusters of observations because income was divided into categories.  I observed that the residuals were not evenly distributed around zero, with many negative residuals and some large positive residuals.
## This supports my findings in Q12 and Q13 that mental-health variable is right-skewed, with majority responding zero mental-health days.  The graph suggest that linear regression may not be satisfied and that income alone does not adequately explain the differences in reported poor mental-health days.

# Model 1 - Normal Q-Q
plot(Q14_model1, which = 2)
## I created another diagnostic graph identifying the Q-Q plot, comparing Model 1's standardized residuals against a normal distribution following expected residuals.  Ideally, the points should fall along the diagonal reference line, but my Q-Q plot had a curved pattern rather than following the diagonal line, meaning my data did not follow the normal distributed residuals.  This is due to my data reporting majority zero poor mental-health days. 
## Model 1 identified a statistically significant association between income and poor mental health day, but the residual distribution did not follow and satisfy the ordinary linear regression.

Q14_model2 <- Q11 %>%

## For model 2, I used lm() for multiple linear regression, added exercise as the second predictor to income.  I think exercise will improve the model's ability to explain differences in reported poor mental-health days.
## I continued income as a numeric category code so it is in line with Model 1.  Exercise remained a categorical variable with Yes and No responses.

### Q14 Discussion: Regression
1. From Q11, I created 3 linear regression models to answer my question regarding the relationship between income, exercise, age, and poor mental-health days.  
- Model 1: Income.  
- Model 2: Income + Exercise.  
- Model 3: Income + Exercise + Age

2. I used the same response variable from Q11 (menthlth)

3. Coefficients and Statistical Significance
- Model 1: used 1 predictor of poor mental-health days, income. It's coefficient = -0.5714, p < 0.001.  A negative income association to poor mental-health days.  The higher the income, it predicted a decrease of 0.57 fewer poor mental-health days.  
- Model 2: used 2 predictors of poor mental-health days, income + exercise. After accounting for exercise the income stats improved coefficient of -0.516, p < 0.001. Also, those that did not exercise have 1.32 more predicted poor mental-health days than those that exercised, their coefficient = 1.3246, p < 0.001.
- Model 3: used 3 predictors of poor mental-health days, income + exercise + age. Income continued negative association to poor mental health days, coefficient -0.5649, p < 0.001. Coefficient for those that did not exercised increased to 1.6816. Age had a ordered factor and had a polynomial contrast among groups.  Age had a downward trend in poor mental-health days across increasing age categories. Model 3's R-squared stats indicated 6.83% variation in poor mental-health days, the highest best R-squared out of the models.  

4. Model diagnostics & interpretations
After creating my models, I used plot() to examine "residuals vs. fitted" and "Q-Q" plots to see if they met assumptions. My residuals was unevenly distributed and showed downward patterns which did not meet how residuals should appear. My models did not fit because of the huge numebr of zero responses that I had.  The Q-Q plots had a reference line, and my data did not follow that line.  Instead my data had a curved pattern, which means my residuals did not fit and distributed unevenly.  Which again is due to the many zero responses. 
-The residual standard error for my models are:
Model 1 = 8.08 days
Model 2 = 8.06 days
Model 3 = 7.91 days.
This showed Model 3 has the best residual standard error, but the range is from 0 to 30 days, which ties back to the many zero responses causing the unusual distribution.

5. Best regression model
To decide which model is best, I used R-squared, AIC, residual standard error (RSE), and ANOVA results to make the determination.

R-squared: Model 1 (0.0284), Model 2 (0.0328), Model 3 (0.0683). Result showed Model 3 had the greatest variation.

AIC: Model 1 (2,380,168), Model 2 (2,378,619), Model 3 (2,365,958)
Result showed Model 3 had the lowest AIC (lowest is the best) 

RSE: Model 1 (8.08), Model 2 (8.06), Model 3 (7.91)
Result showed Model 3 is the best.

ANOVA: Model 1 to Model 2, F-statistic = 1,613.7 (suggesting model improved fit); Model 2 to Model 3, F-statistic = 2,5821 (suggesting better model improved fit)

Based on the results, out of the three choices I decided model 3 was the best performing.  However, all my models have limitations, and my best performing model does not explain 93.17% of my data.  Also, my diagnostic plots due to the large number of zero responses a linear regression would not be the best approach for my variables.

### Q15 Discussion:

1. I chose my best model from Q14_model3 to make my predictions.  Also as a bonus, Q14 Model 3 contained all my predictors: income, exercise, and age. Also, I made sure that they have the same  

2. I first created a data frame listing 3 hypothetical individuals, provided made up random information aligning with categories of my predictors mirroring income, exercise, and age responses. I used factor on age and exercise because I had them set up that way before for R calculations.  I used predict() with Q14_model3 to calculate predictions for poor mental-health days for my 3 hypothetical individuals. I used mutate() to create the column for predicted_menthlth.  I used round() to get whole numbers to align with menthlth data having whole numbers. 
Output:
- Individual 1: Income = 3, Exercise = No, Age = 2, predicted_menthlth = 9
- Individual 2: Income = 7, Exercise = Yes, Age = 3, predicted_menthlth = 5
- Individual 3: Income = 11, Exercise = No, Age = 6, predicted_menthlth = 1

3. Interpretation of predictions
- Individual 1, out of the other two predicted-menthlth results, individual 1 had the highest poor mental-health days.  Individual 1 out of the others hypothetical entries (income 7 & 11), had the lowest income of 3, did not exercise, and younger out of the 3.  This prediction is consistent with my earlier results.  Lower income and younger age had higher poor mental-health observations.

- Individual 2, had predicted_menthlth of 5, Income = 7, exercised, middle age group. Individual 2 was at a higher income category than Individual 1, a little older than individual 1, and exercised.  The predicted-menthlth is consistent with my earlier results and make sense as it had less poor mental health days as Individual 1.

- Individual 3, had the lowest predicted_menthlth = 1.  High income, and oldest age group, but did not exercise.  It's interesting because it considered all three categories and I would say the predicted poor mental health day of 1 is consistent with my earlier results. Higher income and older age had lower poor mental-health reports. 

4. Reliability, limitations of predictions and reliability

Model 3 was the best out of the three models I created.  However, I acknowledge and mentioned earlier that its predictions have many limitations. Model 3 has an R-squared of 0.0683 for income, exercise, and age, only 6.83% ov the variation in poor mental health days, leaving 93.17% unexplained.  Furthermore, the residual standard error was ~ 7.91 days and the residuals did not follow the linear regression assumption.  Moreover, the income and age observations was categorical instead of having exact dollar or year count; the exercise category also had limits with what type of exercise or intensity did they do as the level of physical activity could impact the data. In addition, mental health data was right skewed due to the large number of zero days reported.

Overall, Model 3 was useful in providing predictions and was consistent with the findings from earlier results. I would say the predicted_mnthlth values as approximate predictions and not reliable because of the limitations I listed above.
